name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q01 - Aristotle fallacy regarding motion and external force

questiontext.text: According to Aristotle's view of mechanics, an external force is required to keep a body in uniform motion. What is the fundamental flaw in this reasoning as revealed by Newtonian mechanics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Newtonian mechanics, Galileo's law of inertia establishes that a body in uniform motion with constant velocity experiences zero net external force. Acceleration can be non-zero only if a net external force acts on the body.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
In everyday terrestrial experience, whenever a body moves, opposing resistive forces such as friction between solid surfaces or viscous drag in fluids are naturally present. To keep an object moving uniformly, an external force must be applied continuously to cancel these resistive forces.

Step 3: Application
When a toy car is pulled at a constant speed, the pulling force exactly equals the opposing frictional force, yielding a net force of zero. If friction were completely eliminated, no external force would be required to maintain uniform motion.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Aristotle mistook the practical requirement of countering friction for an intrinsic law of motion. Therefore, the fundamental flaw is that practical motion on Earth experiences resistive forces like friction; an applied force is only needed to balance opposing frictional forces so that the net external force is zero.

Final Conceptual Answer: Practical motion on Earth experiences resistive forces like friction; an applied force is only needed to balance opposing frictional forces so that the net external force is zero.

answer.text: Practical motion on Earth experiences resistive forces like friction; an applied force is only needed to balance opposing frictional forces so that the net external force is zero.
An external force is always needed to continuously accelerate bodies moving with uniform velocity.
Natural terrestrial motion requires constant propulsion because inertia naturally decays with time.
Moving bodies possess an internal store of force that continually opposes the external medium.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q02 - Galileo inclined plane study on horizontal motion

questiontext.text: Galileo deduced the concept of inertia by observing the motion of objects on inclined planes. Which of the following statements correctly summarizes his observation for an object moving along a frictionless horizontal plane?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Galileo observed that objects moving down an inclined plane accelerate, while objects moving up an inclined plane retard. Motion along a horizontal plane represents the intermediate limiting case between acceleration and retardation.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
Since the downward slope causes acceleration and the upward slope causes deceleration, a horizontal plane with zero slope causes neither acceleration nor retardation in the absence of opposing frictional forces.

Step 3: Application
Consequently, on an idealized frictionless horizontal plane, a moving body must continue to move with constant velocity indefinitely.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The state of uniform linear motion is equivalent to the state of rest, both corresponding to zero net force and zero acceleration. Thus, the object experiences neither acceleration nor retardation and continues to move with constant velocity.

Final Conceptual Answer: The object experiences neither acceleration nor retardation and continues to move with constant velocity.

answer.text: The object experiences neither acceleration nor retardation and continues to move with constant velocity.
The object continuously accelerates because there is no friction to oppose it.
The object gradually retards because all horizontal motion naturally tends to rest.
The object requires a small constant horizontal force to sustain its speed.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q03 - Galileo double inclined plane thought experiment limiting case

questiontext.text: In Galileo's thought experiment on a smooth double inclined plane, a ball released from rest on one plane rolls down and climbs up the opposing plane. When the slope of the second plane is reduced to zero (a horizontal plane), what ideal trajectory does the ball follow in the absence of friction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
On a smooth double inclined plane, a rolling ball released from rest reaches the same vertical height on the opposing plane. Decreasing the slope of the second plane requires the ball to travel a longer distance along the plane to attain that same initial height.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
In the limiting case where the slope of the second plane is reduced to zero, the plane becomes horizontal and the ball can never reach its original vertical height.

Step 3: Application
Because the ball can never achieve the original height on a horizontal plane, its motion never ceases in the absence of friction. It travels an infinite distance at a constant velocity.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
In this idealized frictionless situation, the motion continues indefinitely. Thus, the ball continues to move indefinitely along the horizontal plane with constant velocity, never coming to rest.

Final Conceptual Answer: It continues to move indefinitely along the horizontal plane with constant velocity, never coming to rest.

answer.text: It continues to move indefinitely along the horizontal plane with constant velocity, never coming to rest.
It travels a finite distance proportional to the initial release height and then stops.
It accelerates indefinitely along the horizontal plane due to gravity.
It comes to rest when its kinetic energy is completely exhausted by internal resistance.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q04 - Quantitative measure of inertia of a material body

questiontext.text: The property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia. Which physical quantity is the quantitative measure of the inertia of a body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inertia is the inherent resistance of any material body to a change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Newton's first law defines this property qualitatively.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
A greater force is required to impart the same acceleration to a more massive body than to a less massive body. For example, pushing a loaded truck requires vastly greater force than pushing a small car to produce equal acceleration in equal time.

Step 3: Application
In Newtonian mechanics, the mass of a body determines how strongly it resists acceleration when acted upon by a given external force according to \( \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} \).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The quantitative measure of the inertia of a material body is its mass.

Final Conceptual Answer: Mass

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q05 - Net force acting on falling terminal raindrop

questiontext.text: A raindrop of mass \(m\) falls vertically downward through the atmosphere with a constant terminal velocity. What is the magnitude of the net external force acting on the raindrop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's first law of motion, if a body moves with a constant velocity in a straight line (uniform motion), its acceleration is identically zero.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The acceleration of the raindrop is given by \( \mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \). By Newton's second law, \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\mathbf{a} \).

Step 3: Application
Since \( \mathbf{a} = 0 \), the net external force must be \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m(0) = 0 \). The upward viscous drag and buoyant force of the air exactly balance the downward gravitational pull of the Earth.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The forces are in complete equilibrium during terminal motion. Thus, the magnitude of the net external force acting on the raindrop is zero.

Final Conceptual Answer: Zero

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q06 - Net force on vertically projected pebble at apex

questiontext.text: A pebble of mass \(0.05\text{ kg}\) is thrown vertically upwards into the air. Neglecting air resistance and taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the magnitude and direction of the net force acting on the pebble at the highest point of its trajectory where it is momentarily at rest?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the pebble: \(m = 0.05\text{ kg}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\) downwards. State of motion at the apex: instantaneous speed \(v = 0\). Air resistance is neglected.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Vertical direction: take downwards as the positive direction or standard directional description. The pebble is in free flight under Earth's gravity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Newton's second law, \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\mathbf{a} \). In free flight without air resistance, the only force acting on the pebble at all times is gravity, so \( \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{g} \) downwards.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Even though the velocity is momentarily zero at the highest point, the acceleration remains non-zero and equal to \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\) downwards. Therefore: \(F_{\text{net}} = m g = 0.05\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 0.5\text{ N}\), directed vertically downwards.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Zero velocity does not imply zero force or zero acceleration; gravitational attraction is continuous. Thus, the net force is \(0.5\text{ N}\) directed vertically downwards.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.5\text{ N}\) directed vertically downwards

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q07 - Acceleration of astronaut separated from accelerating spaceship

questiontext.text: An astronaut accidentally gets separated out of a small spaceship that is accelerating in interstellar space at a constant rate of \(100\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Assuming there are no nearby celestial bodies and the gravitational attraction of the spaceship is negligible, what is the acceleration of the astronaut immediately after being outside the spaceship?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's second law, acceleration is determined by the net external force acting on the body here and now (local relation). A body does not retain or carry forward the acceleration or force of its past environment.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
Once outside the spaceship, the astronaut is no longer in contact with the spaceship, so the thrust of the rocket engines can no longer exert any contact force on the astronaut. Furthermore, all external gravitational forces from celestial bodies and the spaceship are negligible.

Step 3: Application
The net external force acting on the astronaut is \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = 0 \). According to Newton's first law of motion, if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The astronaut continues to move with the velocity acquired at the instant of separation, but experiences zero acceleration. Thus, the acceleration of the astronaut immediately after being outside the spaceship is zero.

Final Conceptual Answer: Zero

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q08 - Backward jerk experienced by passengers on sudden start

questiontext.text: When a stationary bus suddenly accelerates forward, standing passengers tend to fall backward relative to the bus. Which physical principle correctly explains this backward jerk?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's first law of motion, every body continues in its state of rest unless compelled by an external force to change that state (inertia of rest).

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The feet of the passenger are in contact with the floor of the bus. Friction between the feet and the floor provides the forward force necessary to accelerate the feet along with the bus.

Step 3: Application
Because the human body is deformable rather than strictly rigid, the upper part of the body tends to remain in its initial position of rest due to inertia. Consequently, relative to the accelerating bus frame, the upper body falls backward until muscular forces restore equilibrium.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The phenomenon is an immediate consequence of inertia of rest. Thus, the inertia of rest of the upper body keeps it in its initial position while friction accelerates the feet forward with the bus floor.

Final Conceptual Answer: The inertia of rest of the upper body keeps it in its initial position while friction accelerates the feet forward with the bus floor.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q09 - Forward jerk experienced by passengers on sudden braking

questiontext.text: When a rapidly moving bus suddenly applies brakes and stops, standing passengers are thrown forward. What is the fundamental cause of this forward motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's first law of motion, a body in uniform motion continues to move with constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force (inertia of motion).

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
When brakes are applied, the floor of the bus decelerates. Frictional forces between the passenger's feet and the floor bring the feet to rest along with the bus.

Step 3: Application
Due to inertia of motion, the rest of the body continues moving forward at the original speed because no external braking force acts directly on the upper body. Relative to the bus, the passenger is therefore thrown forward until muscular and support forces arrest the motion.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The forward tilt is caused by the inertia of motion of the upper body. Thus, the inertia of motion causes the upper body to continue moving forward while friction brings the feet to rest with the floor.

Final Conceptual Answer: The inertia of motion causes the upper body to continue moving forward while friction brings the feet to rest with the floor.

answer.text: The inertia of motion causes the upper body to continue moving forward while friction brings the feet to rest with the floor.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q10 - Action reaction pair identification for book on table

questiontext.text: A book of weight \(W = mg\) rests at equilibrium on a horizontal table. The table exerts an upward normal force \(R\) on the book such that \(R = W\). Which of the following constitutes the true Newton's third law reaction to the downward gravitational pull of the Earth on the book?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's third law of motion, forces always occur in mutual action-reaction pairs between two distinct interacting bodies. If body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The downward gravitational pull \(W\) is a force exerted on the book by the Earth. By Newton's third law, its reaction must be a force exerted on the Earth by the book.

Step 3: Application
The upward normal force \(R\) is exerted on the book by the table, and its reaction is the downward force exerted by the book on the table. The equality \(R = W\) is a consequence of translational equilibrium (Newton's first law for the book), not Newton's third law, because both \(R\) and \(W\) act on the same body (the book).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Action and reaction must act on different interacting bodies. Thus, the reaction to the downward gravitational pull of the Earth on the book is the upward gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth.

Final Conceptual Answer: The upward gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth

answer.text: The upward gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth
The upward normal reaction force exerted by the table on the book
The downward contact force exerted by the book on the table
The static frictional force between the book and the table surface

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q11 - Horizontal force on stone dropped from accelerating train

questiontext.text: A train is moving horizontally along a straight track with a constant acceleration of \(1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). A passenger drops a stone of mass \(0.2\text{ kg}\) from the window. Just after the stone is released, what is the magnitude of the net horizontal force acting on the stone, neglecting air resistance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the stone: \(m = 0.2\text{ kg}\). Acceleration of the train prior to release: \(a_{\text{train}} = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Air resistance is neglected.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coordinate system: horizontal axis along the track, vertical axis pointing downward. Motion is considered immediately after release into the air.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Newton's second law, acceleration and force are local in time: \( \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} \). A body does not carry any memory of previous forces once contact with the accelerating agency ceases.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The moment the stone is released from the passenger's hand, there is no horizontal contact force between the train and the stone. Since air resistance is neglected, the only material agency exerting a force on the stone is the Earth (gravitational pull \(mg\) directed vertically downwards). Consequently, the net horizontal force is \(F_x = 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The stone retains its horizontal velocity at the instant of release due to inertia, but experiences zero horizontal force and therefore zero horizontal acceleration. Thus, the magnitude of the net horizontal force is zero.

Final Conceptual Answer: Zero

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q12 - Horizontal frictional force on stone on train floor

questiontext.text: A stone of mass \(0.1\text{ kg}\) lies on the horizontal floor of a train that is accelerating uniformly along a straight track at \(1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). The stone remains completely at rest relative to the floor of the train. What is the magnitude of the net horizontal force acting on the stone?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of stone: \(m = 0.1\text{ kg}\). Acceleration of the train: \(a = 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). State of motion: stone is stationary relative to the train floor.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Ground frame of reference (inertial frame). In this frame, the stone accelerates along with the train with acceleration \(a = 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Newton's second law: \(F_{\text{net}, x} = m a_x\). In the horizontal direction, static friction \(f_s\) between the stone and the floor accelerates the stone.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into Newton's second law: \(F_{\text{net}, x} = m a = 0.1\text{ kg} \times 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2} = 0.1\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The static friction provides exactly the force needed to accelerate the stone with the train. Thus, the magnitude of the net horizontal force acting on the stone is \(0.1\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.1\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q13 - Average resistive force on stopped bullet in block

questiontext.text: A bullet of mass \(0.04\text{ kg}\) moving with an initial speed of \(90\text{ m s}^{-1}\) enters a heavy wooden block and is brought to rest over a penetration distance of \(60\text{ cm}\). What is the magnitude of the average retarding force exerted by the block on the bullet?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of bullet: \(m = 0.04\text{ kg}\). Initial speed: \(u = 90\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Penetration distance: \(s = 60\text{ cm} = 0.60\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume uniform average deceleration \(a\) along the straight line of penetration.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Kinematic equation relating velocity and distance: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Newton's second law: \(F_{\text{retarding}} = m |a|\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the acceleration: \(0 = 90^2 + 2 \times a \times 0.60 \implies 1.2 a = -8100 \implies a = -\frac{8100}{1.2} = -6750\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Now compute the average retarding force: \(F = m |a| = 0.04\text{ kg} \times 6750\text{ m s}^{-2} = 270\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check units: \(\text{kg} \times \text{m s}^{-2} = \text{N}\). The magnitude is \(270\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(270\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q14 - Net force on particle with quadratic position equation

questiontext.text: The vertical position of a particle of mass \(m\) moving near the Earth's surface as a function of time \(t\) is described by \(y(t) = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2\), where \(u\) and \(g\) are constants. According to Newton's second law of motion, what is the net force acting on the particle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of particle: \(m\). Position function: \(y(t) = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2\). Constants: \(u\) (initial velocity) and \(g\) (acceleration parameter).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is one-dimensional along the \(y\)-axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity is the first time derivative of position: \(v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\). Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity: \(a(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\). Force by Newton's second law: \(F = ma\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiate position with respect to time: \(v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2\right) = u + gt\). Differentiate velocity to obtain acceleration: \(a(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(u + gt) = g\). Multiply by mass to obtain force: \(F = m a = m g\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The acceleration is constant and equals \(g\), which corresponds to the downward gravitational force. Thus, the net force acting on the particle is \(mg\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(mg\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q15 - Impulse imparted to cricket ball struck straight back

questiontext.text: A batsman hits back a ball of mass \(0.15\text{ kg}\) straight in the direction of the bowler without changing its initial speed of \(12\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Assuming linear motion, what is the magnitude of the impulse imparted to the ball by the bat?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of cricket ball: \(m = 0.15\text{ kg}\). Initial speed: \(u = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}\) in the directly opposite direction.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the initial direction of motion (from bowler to batsman) be the positive \(x\)-direction. The reversed direction (from batsman to bowler) is the negative \(x\)-direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Impulse is defined as the change in momentum: \( \mathbf{I} = \Delta \mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} - m\mathbf{u} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Initial momentum: \(p_i = m u = 0.15\text{ kg} \times (+12\text{ m s}^{-1}) = +1.8\text{ N s}\). Final momentum: \(p_f = m v = 0.15\text{ kg} \times (-12\text{ m s}^{-1}) = -1.8\text{ N s}\). Change in momentum: \(\Delta p = p_f - p_i = -1.8 - (+1.8) = -3.6\text{ N s}\). Magnitude of impulse: \(|I| = 3.6\text{ N s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude of the change in momentum is \(2mu = 2 \times 0.15 \times 12 = 3.6\text{ N s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(3.6\text{ N s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q16 - Mechanics of cricketer drawing hands back catching ball

questiontext.text: A seasoned cricketer draws their hands backward while catching a fast-moving cricket ball. How does this technique reduce the impact force on the hands?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Impulse equals the change in momentum: \( \mathbf{I} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{avg}} \Delta t = \Delta \mathbf{p} \).

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
To catch a ball of mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(v\), the hands must bring its momentum to zero, meaning \(\Delta p = mv\) is fixed by the initial state of the ball.

Step 3: Application
By drawing the hands backward in the direction of the ball's motion, the fielder increases the time duration \(\Delta t\) over which the momentum change occurs. Because \(F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), increasing \(\Delta t\) dramatically decreases the average force \(F_{\text{avg}}\) exerted on the hands, preventing pain and injury.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total momentum change remains identical, but the rate of change of momentum is reduced. Thus, the technique works by increasing the time taken to bring the momentum of the ball to zero, thereby decreasing the rate of change of momentum.

Final Conceptual Answer: By increasing the time taken to bring the momentum of the ball to zero, thereby decreasing the rate of change of momentum.

By decreasing the total change in momentum required to stop the ball.

By reducing the mass of the ball during the impact duration.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q17 - Component independence in vector Newton second law

questiontext.text: A particle is projected horizontally with an initial speed \(u_x\) in a region where a uniform vertical gravitational force \(mg\) acts downwards. Which component of the velocity changes with time, and what happens to the horizontal component of velocity in the absence of air resistance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Newton's second law is a vector law: \( \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} \). In Cartesian components, this is equivalent to three independent equations: \(F_x = m a_x\), \(F_y = m a_y\), and \(F_z = m a_z\).

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
A force acting along one direction changes only the component of velocity parallel to that force; the perpendicular velocity components remain completely unaffected.

Step 3: Application
Here, gravity acts strictly vertically downwards (\(F_y = -mg\)), so \(a_y = -g\) causes the vertical velocity component \(v_y\) to change continuously with time. In the horizontal direction, there is no applied force (\(F_x = 0\)), which means \(a_x = 0\) and the horizontal velocity component remains constant at \(u_x\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Each component evolves independently according to its corresponding component of net force. Thus, only the vertical component of velocity changes with time; the horizontal component remains constant because the net horizontal force is zero.

Final Conceptual Answer: Only the vertical component of velocity changes with time; the horizontal component remains constant because the net horizontal force is zero.

answer.text: Only the vertical component of velocity changes with time; the horizontal component remains constant because the net horizontal force is zero.
Both horizontal and vertical components of velocity decrease steadily with time.
The horizontal velocity increases while the vertical velocity remains constant.
The horizontal velocity decreases to zero as the vertical velocity increases.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q18 - Local relationship property of Newton second law

questiontext.text: Newton's second law of motion is described as a 'local relation'. What does this fundamental property imply about the acceleration of a particle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Newtonian mechanics, the equation \( \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}, t) = m\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}, t) \) relates the force acting on a particle at a specific location \(\mathbf{r}\) and instant \(t\) to its acceleration at that same location and instant.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The acceleration of a body here and now is determined strictly by the net external force acting on it here and now. The body does not carry any residual 'force' or memory of its past motion.

Step 3: Application
For instance, the instant a stone is dropped from an accelerating train, it ceases to experience any horizontal acceleration from the train because the contact force has ceased, despite having moved with the train previously.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Past kinematics do not determine present acceleration. Thus, the acceleration of a particle at a given point and instant is determined solely by the net external force acting on it at that exact point and instant, independent of its past motion.

Final Conceptual Answer: The acceleration of a particle at a given point and instant is determined solely by the net external force acting on it at that exact point and instant, independent of its past motion.

answer.text: The acceleration of a particle at a given point and instant is determined solely by the net external force acting on it at that exact point and instant, independent of its past motion.
The acceleration depends on the accumulated historical work done on the particle along its path.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q19 - Stopping time for body under retarding force

questiontext.text: A constant retarding force of \(50\text{ N}\) is applied to a body of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) moving initially with a speed of \(15\text{ m s}^{-1}\). How long does the body take to come to a complete stop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 20\text{ kg}\). Initial velocity: \(u = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final velocity: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Retarding force: \(F = -50\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the direction of initial velocity be positive. The retarding force acts in the negative direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Newton's second law: \(a = \frac{F}{m}\). Kinematic relation for stopping time: \(v = u + at \implies t = \frac{v - u}{a}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute deceleration: \(a = \frac{-50\text{ N}}{20\text{ kg}} = -2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Compute stopping time: \(t = \frac{0 - 15\text{ m s}^{-1}}{-2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}} = 6.0\text{ s}\). Alternatively, using impulse: \(F \Delta t = m(0 - u) \implies (-50) t = 20(-15) = -300 \implies t = 6.0\text{ s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The time is positive and physically sensible: \(t = 6.0\text{ s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(6.0\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q20 - Constant force altering speed of moving body

questiontext.text: A constant force acting on a body of mass \(3.0\text{ kg}\) changes its speed from \(2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) to \(3.5\text{ m s}^{-1}\) in \(25\text{ s}\) without altering its direction of motion. What is the magnitude of the applied force?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the body: \(m = 3.0\text{ kg}\). Initial speed: \(u = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 3.5\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Time interval: \(\Delta t = 25\text{ s}\). Direction is unchanged.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is in a constant straight line direction (taken as positive). Force acts in the direction of motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Acceleration: \(a = \frac{v - u}{\Delta t}\). Newton's second law: \(F = m a = m \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the acceleration: \(a = \frac{3.5\text{ m s}^{-1} - 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}}{25\text{ s}} = \frac{1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}}{25\text{ s}} = 0.06\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Calculate the force: \(F = 3.0\text{ kg} \times 0.06\text{ m s}^{-2} = 0.18\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check units: \(\text{kg} \times \text{m s}^{-2} = \text{N}\). The force is \(0.18\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.18\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q21 - Acceleration of body under two mutually perpendicular forces

questiontext.text: A body of mass \(5\text{ kg}\) initially at rest is acted upon simultaneously by two mutually perpendicular forces of magnitude \(8\text{ N}\) and \(6\text{ N}\). What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the body: \(m = 5\text{ kg}\). Forces: \(F_1 = 8\text{ N}\) and \(F_2 = 6\text{ N}\) acting at an angle of \(90^\circ\) to each other.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The forces act in a plane concurrently on the center of mass of the body.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resultant of two perpendicular forces: \(F_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2}\). Newton's second law: \(a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate resultant force magnitude: \(F_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ N}\). Calculate acceleration: \(a = \frac{10\text{ N}}{5\text{ kg}} = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The 6-8-10 Pythagorean triple gives \(10\text{ N}\), leading directly to \(a = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q22 - Average retarding force stopping three wheeler for child

questiontext.text: A three-wheeler moving with a speed of \(36\text{ km h}^{-1}\) is brought to rest uniformly in \(4.0\text{ s}\). The combined mass of the vehicle and the driver is \(465\text{ kg}\). What is the magnitude of the average retarding force acting on the vehicle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(u = 36\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Stopping time: \(\Delta t = 4.0\text{ s}\). Total mass of system: \(m = 400\text{ kg} + 65\text{ kg} = 465\text{ kg}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Convert speed to SI units: \(u = 36 \times \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration is uniform.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Retardation: \(a = \frac{v - u}{\Delta t}\). Average retarding force: \(F_{\text{ret}} = m |a|\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate deceleration: \(a = \frac{0 - 10\text{ m s}^{-1}}{4.0\text{ s}} = -2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Calculate retarding force magnitude: \(F_{\text{ret}} = 465\text{ kg} \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} = 1162.5\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying \(465\) by \(2.5\) yields \(1162.5\text{ N}\). Thus, the average retarding force is \(1162.5\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(1162.5\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q23 - Initial blast off thrust for vertically accelerating rocket

questiontext.text: A rocket with a lift-off mass of \(20{,}000\text{ kg}\) is blasted vertically upwards with an initial acceleration of \(5.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the initial thrust force exerted by the blast?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of rocket: \(m = 20{,}000\text{ kg}\). Upward acceleration: \(a = 5.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Vertical direction is chosen as the positive axis. The upward forces are thrust \(F_{\text{thrust}}\) and the downward force is gravity \(mg\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Newton's second law: \(F_{\text{net}} = m a \implies F_{\text{thrust}} - m g = m a\). Therefore, \(F_{\text{thrust}} = m(g + a)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the total effective upward acceleration: \(g + a = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} + 5.0\text{ m s}^{-2} = 15.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Compute thrust force: \(F_{\text{thrust}} = 20{,}000\text{ kg} \times 15.0\text{ m s}^{-2} = 300{,}000\text{ N} = 3.0 \times 10^5\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The thrust must overcome weight (\(2.0 \times 10^5\text{ N}\)) and provide accelerating force (\(1.0 \times 10^5\text{ N}\)), totaling \(3.0 \times 10^5\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(3.0 \times 10^5\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q24 - Trajectory of oscillating pendulum bob when string cut

questiontext.text: A pendulum bob oscillates back and forth in a vertical plane. What are the trajectories of the bob if the string is cut when the bob is at its extreme position and at its mean position, respectively?

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When the string is cut, the tension vanishes instantly and the only force acting on the bob is gravity. The subsequent path depends on the instantaneous velocity vector at the moment the constraint is removed.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
At an extreme position of oscillation, the bob comes momentarily to rest, so its instantaneous velocity is zero (\(v = 0\)). Released from rest under gravity, it falls straight down along a vertical line.

Step 3: Application
At the mean position, the bob has purely horizontal velocity of maximum magnitude (\(v = v_{\max}\hat{i}\)). When released with horizontal velocity under vertical gravitational acceleration \(g\), it becomes a horizontal projectile, describing a parabolic trajectory.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
At the extreme position the initial velocity is zero giving free fall, while at the mean position the initial velocity is horizontal giving projectile motion. Thus, the trajectories are a vertically downward straight line at the extreme position and a parabolic path at the mean position.

Final Conceptual Answer: Vertically downward straight line at the extreme position; parabolic path at the mean position.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q25 - Disintegration of stationary radioactive nucleus into two fragments

questiontext.text: A stationary radioactive nucleus in its rest frame spontaneously disintegrates into two daughter nuclei of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\). If the speed of the first fragment is \(v_1\), what must be the velocity of the second fragment?

Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial state: parent nucleus at rest, so total initial momentum \( \mathbf{p}_i = 0 \). Final state: two fragments of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) with velocities \( \mathbf{v}_1 \) and \( \mathbf{v}_2 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
No external forces act during the spontaneous disintegration (isolated system).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Law of conservation of linear momentum: \( \mathbf{p}_f = \mathbf{p}_i \implies m_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + m_2 \mathbf{v}_2 = 0 \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The momentum vectors are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Thus, the second fragment moves in the direction opposite to the first fragment with a speed of \(\frac{m_1}{m_2} v_1\).

Final Conceptual Answer: Directed oppositely to the first fragment with a speed of \(\frac{m_1}{m_2} v_1\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q26 - Impulse exchanged between identical colliding billiard balls

questiontext.text: Two identical billiard balls, each of mass \(0.05\text{ kg}\), moving in opposite directions along a straight line with a speed of \(6\text{ m s}^{-1}\), collide head-on and rebound elastically with the same speed. What is the magnitude of the impulse imparted to each ball by the other?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of each ball: \(m = 0.05\text{ kg}\). Initial speed: \(u = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Rebound speed: \(v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}\) in the opposite direction.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For one ball, choose its initial direction of motion as positive. Its post-collision direction is negative.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Impulse is equal to change in momentum: \(I = \Delta p = m(v - u)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Initial momentum: \(p_i = 0.05\text{ kg} \times (+6\text{ m s}^{-1}) = +0.3\text{ N s}\). Final momentum: \(p_f = 0.05\text{ kg} \times (-6\text{ m s}^{-1}) = -0.3\text{ N s}\). Impulse: \(\Delta p = -0.3 - (+0.3) = -0.6\text{ N s}\). The magnitude of the impulse is \(|I| = 0.6\text{ N s}\). By Newton's third law, the other ball experiences an equal and opposite impulse of magnitude \(0.6\text{ N s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(2mu = 2 \times 0.05 \times 6 = 0.6\text{ N s}\). The magnitude of impulse is \(0.6\text{ N s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q27 - Recoil speed of gun firing shell horizontally

questiontext.text: A shell of mass \(0.020\text{ kg}\) is fired horizontally by a gun of mass \(100\text{ kg}\). If the muzzle speed of the shell is \(80\text{ m s}^{-1}\), what is the recoil speed of the gun?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of shell: \(m = 0.020\text{ kg}\). Muzzle speed of shell: \(v_{\text{shell}} = 80\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Mass of gun: \(M = 100\text{ kg}\). Initial state: both gun and shell are at rest.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The system (gun + shell) is isolated along the horizontal axis during firing. Direction of the fired shell is positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Law of conservation of momentum: \(P_{\text{total}} = 0 \implies M V_{\text{recoil}} + m v_{\text{shell}} = 0 \implies V_{\text{recoil}} = -\frac{m v_{\text{shell}}}{M}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute values: \(V_{\text{recoil}} = -\frac{0.020\text{ kg} \times 80\text{ m s}^{-1}}{100\text{ kg}} = -\frac{1.6}{100} = -0.016\text{ m s}^{-1}\). The recoil speed (magnitude) is \(0.016\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Check units: \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). The speed is \(0.016\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q28 - Trajectory of whirling stone when string suddenly snaps

questiontext.text: A stone tied to the end of a string is whirled in a horizontal circle. If the string suddenly breaks during the rotation, which of the following accurately describes the trajectory of the stone immediately after the break?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In circular motion, the velocity vector of the particle is directed tangentially to the circular path at every instant. The centripetal force is provided solely by the tension in the string directed radially inward.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The moment the string breaks, the inward tension becomes zero immediately. In the absence of an inward radial force, no force acts along the horizontal plane.

Step 3: Application
By Newton's first law of motion, in the absence of a net horizontal force, the stone must continue to move in a straight line with the velocity it possessed at the exact instant the string broke, which is directed tangentially to the circle.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
There is no outward force (centrifugal force is not a real force in an inertial frame). Thus, the stone flies off tangentially to the circular path from the instant the string breaks.

Final Conceptual Answer: It flies off tangentially to the circular path from the instant the string breaks.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q29 - Maximum acceleration of train keeping resting box stationary

questiontext.text: A box rests on the horizontal floor of an accelerating train. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is \(\mu_s = 0.15\). Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the maximum acceleration of the train such that the box remains stationary relative to the train floor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Coefficient of static friction: \(\mu_s = 0.15\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Condition: box remains stationary relative to the train floor.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the vertical direction, the box is in equilibrium: \(N = mg\). In the horizontal direction, static friction \(f_s\) accelerates the box.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equation of motion: \(f_s = ma\). Static friction constraint: \(f_s \le (f_s)_{\max} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg\). Therefore, \(ma \le \mu_s mg \implies a \le \mu_s g\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the maximum acceleration: \(a_{\max} = \mu_s g = 0.15 \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The mass cancels out, showing the threshold acceleration depends purely on \(\mu_s\) and \(g\). Thus, the maximum acceleration of the train is \(1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q30 - Coefficient of static friction from limiting incline angle

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(4\text{ kg}\) rests on a plane that is gradually inclined to the horizontal. At an angle of inclination \(\theta = 15^\circ\), the block just begins to slide down the plane. What is the coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s\) between the block and the surface? (Given \(\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.27\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of block: \(m = 4\text{ kg}\). Limiting angle of inclination (angle of repose): \(\theta = 15^\circ\). Value given: \(\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.27\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coordinate axes: along the inclined plane (parallel) and perpendicular to the inclined plane.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Forces acting on the block: weight resolved into \(mg \sin\theta\) down the incline and \(mg \cos\theta\) normal into the plane; normal force \(N = mg \cos\theta\); maximum static friction \((f_s)_{\max} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg \cos\theta\). At impending motion: \(mg \sin\theta = \mu_s mg \cos\theta \implies \mu_s = \tan\theta\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the angle of repose: \(\mu_s = \tan 15^\circ = 0.27\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The coefficient of static friction is dimensionless and independent of the mass of the block. Thus, \(\mu_s = 0.27\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.27\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q31 - Rationale for pulling lawn mower versus pushing it

questiontext.text: When moving a lawn mower, why is pulling it at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal mechanically easier than pushing it at the same angle \(\theta\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kinetic frictional force is proportional to the normal reaction: \(f_k = \mu_k N\). Any alteration in the normal reaction force directly alters the frictional resistance opposing horizontal motion.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
When pulling with an applied force \(F\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, the vertical component is upward (\(F \sin\theta\)), giving vertical equilibrium \(N_{\text{pull}} = mg - F \sin\theta\). Thus, \(N_{\text{pull}} < mg\), which reduces the friction to \(f_{\text{pull}} = \mu_k (mg - F \sin\theta)\).

Step 3: Application
When pushing with force \(F\) at angle \(\theta\) below the horizontal, the vertical component is downward (\(F \sin\theta\)), giving \(N_{\text{push}} = mg + F \sin\theta\). Thus, \(N_{\text{push}} > mg\), which increases the friction to \(f_{\text{push}} = \mu_k (mg + F \sin\theta)\). Because \(f_{\text{pull}} < f_{\text{push}}\), pulling requires smaller horizontal effort than pushing.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Pulling relieves the normal reaction while pushing increases it. Thus, the vertical component of the pulling force acts upward, reducing the normal reaction and kinetic friction; while pushing adds a downward component, increasing normal reaction and friction.

Final Conceptual Answer: The vertical component of the pulling force acts upward, reducing the normal reaction and kinetic friction; while pushing adds a downward component, increasing normal reaction and friction.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q32 - Slipping condition for turning cyclist on level road

questiontext.text: A cyclist travels at a speed of \(18\text{ km h}^{-1}\) on a level road and takes a sharp circular turn of radius \(3\text{ m}\) without reducing speed. generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of circular turn: \(R = 3\text{ m}\). Speed of cyclist: \(v = 18\text{ km h}^{-1} = 18 \times \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Coefficient of static friction: \(\mu_s = 0.10\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is on a horizontal flat unbanked road where friction alone provides the centripetal acceleration.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Condition to avoid slipping on a level road: \(v^2 \le \mu_s R g \implies v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s R g}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the threshold: \(\mu_s R g = 0.10 \times 3\text{ m} \times 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} = 2.94\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). The square of the actual speed is: \(v^2 = 5^2 = 25\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). Since \(25 > 2.94\), the condition \(v^2 \le \mu_s R g\) is violated, so the cyclist will slip. The maximum safe speed is \(v_{\max} = \sqrt{2.94}\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 1.71\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The available centripetal force from friction is insufficient for \(v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Thus, the cyclist will slip; the maximum safe speed is \(\sqrt{2.94}\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 1.71\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: The cyclist will slip; the maximum safe speed is \(\sqrt{2.94}\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 1.71\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q33 - Optimum vehicle speed on frictionless banked racetrack

questiontext.text: A circular racetrack of radius \(300\text{ m}\) is banked at an angle of \(\theta = 15^\circ\). Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.268\), what is the optimum speed \(v_0\) at which a race-car can navigate the turn with zero lateral frictional force on its tyres?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of track: \(R = 300\text{ m}\). Banking angle: \(\theta = 15^\circ\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Trigonometric value: \(\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.268\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At the optimum speed \(v_0\), the horizontal component of normal reaction entirely provides the required centripetal acceleration, so lateral friction is zero (\(f = 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Vertical equilibrium: \(N \cos\theta = mg\). Centripetal force: \(N \sin\theta = \frac{m v_0^2}{R}\). Dividing equations gives: \(\tan\theta = \frac{v_0^2}{R g} \implies v_0 = \sqrt{R g \tan\theta}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate: \(v_0^2 = 300\text{ m} \times 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 0.268 = 2940 \times 0.268 \approx 787.92\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). Taking the square root: \(v_0 = \sqrt{787.92} \approx 28.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check units: \(\sqrt{\text{m} \times \text{m s}^{-2}} = \text{m s}^{-1}\). Thus, the optimum speed is \(28.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(28.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q34 - Maximum permissible speed on banked circular racetrack

questiontext.text: A circular racetrack of radius \(R = 300\text{ m}\) is banked at an angle \(\theta = 15^\circ\) (with \(\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.268\)). If the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is \(\mu_s = 0.20\) and \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the maximum permissible speed \(v_{\max}\) to avoid skidding outward?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of track: \(R = 300\text{ m}\). Banking angle: \(\theta = 15^\circ\), \(\tan 15^\circ = 0.268\). Coefficient of friction: \(\mu_s = 0.20\). \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At maximum speed, impending motion is up the banked plane, so limiting friction \(f_s = \mu_s N\) acts downward along the inclined surface.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Maximum speed on a banked road with friction: \(v_{\max} = \sqrt{R g \left(\frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s \tan\theta}\right)}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Numerator: \(\mu_s + \tan\theta = 0.20 + 0.268 = 0.468\). Denominator: \(1 - \mu_s \tan\theta = 1 - (0.20 \times 0.268) = 1 - 0.0536 = 0.9464\). Ratio: \(\frac{0.468}{0.9464} \approx 0.4945\). Now multiply by \(R g\): \(R g = 300 \times 9.8 = 2940\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). \(v_{\max}^2 = 2940 \times 0.4945 \approx 1453.8\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). Take square root: \(v_{\max} = \sqrt{1453.8} \approx 38.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The maximum speed (\(38.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\)) is greater than the optimum speed (\(28.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\)), as expected. Thus, the maximum permissible speed is \(38.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(38.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q35 - Ratio of impulses on reflected billiard balls

questiontext.text: Two identical billiard balls strike a rigid vertical wall with the same speed \(u\). Ball 1 strikes normally and rebounds along the normal with speed \(u\). Ball 2 strikes at an angle of \(30^\circ\) to the normal and reflects specularly with speed \(u\) at \(30^\circ\) to the normal. What is the ratio of the magnitude of impulse imparted to Ball 1 to that imparted to Ball 2 by the wall?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of each ball: \(m\). Speed before and after collision: \(u\). Case 1: normal impact (angle with normal is \(0^\circ\)). Case 2: oblique impact at angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\) to the normal.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the \(x\)-axis be perpendicular to the wall (normal) pointing away from the wall, and the \(y\)-axis be parallel to the surface of the wall.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Impulse is the change in the momentum vector: \( \mathbf{I} = \Delta \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_f - \mathbf{p}_i \). In elastic reflection from a smooth rigid wall, the parallel component of momentum is conserved (\(\Delta p_y = 0\)), and only the normal component reverses sign.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For Ball 1: \(p_{ix} = -mu\), \(p_{fx} = +mu\). Thus, \(I_1 = |\Delta p_x| = mu - (-mu) = 2mu\). For Ball 2: \(p_{ix} = -mu\cos 30^\circ\), \(p_{fx} = +mu\cos 30^\circ\). Thus, \(I_2 = |\Delta p_x| = 2mu \cos 30^\circ = 2mu \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3}mu\). Ratio of impulses: \(\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \frac{2mu}{\sqrt{3}mu} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.155\) matches the ratio of normal momentum changes. Thus, the ratio of the magnitude of impulses is \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q36 - Equilibrium angle of suspended rope with lateral force

questiontext.text: A mass of \(6\text{ kg}\) is suspended from the ceiling by a light rope of length \(2\text{ m}\). A horizontal force of \(50\text{ N}\) is applied at the midpoint \(P\) of the rope. In static equilibrium, taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the tangent of the angle \(\theta\) that the upper segment of the rope makes with the vertical?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Suspended mass: \(M = 6\text{ kg}\). Horizontal force applied at midpoint \(P\): \(F = 50\text{ N}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Rope is light and massless.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coordinate axes: horizontal \(x\)-axis and vertical \(y\)-axis. Tension in upper segment is \(T_1\) at angle \(\theta\) to the vertical. Tension in lower segment is \(T_2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Condition for translational equilibrium of a point particle: \(\sum F_x = 0\) and \(\sum F_y = 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For the suspended mass: \(T_2 = M g = 6\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 60\text{ N}\). For midpoint \(P\): vertical equilibrium gives \(T_1 \cos\theta = T_2 = 60\text{ N}\); horizontal equilibrium gives \(T_1 \sin\theta = F = 50\text{ N}\). Dividing the horizontal equation by the vertical equation: \(\frac{T_1 \sin\theta}{T_1 \cos\theta} = \frac{50\text{ N}}{60\text{ N}} \implies \tan\theta = \frac{5}{6}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The angle does not depend on the length of the rope. Thus, the tangent of the angle is \(\frac{5}{6}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\frac{5}{6}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q37 - Acceleration and tension in block trolley system

questiontext.text: A trolley of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) on a horizontal table is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley to a hanging block of mass \(3\text{ kg}\). The coefficient of kinetic friction between the trolley and the table is \(\mu_k = 0.04\). Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of trolley: \(M = 20\text{ kg}\). Mass of hanging block: \(m = 3\text{ kg}\). Coefficient of kinetic friction: \(\mu_k = 0.04\). \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Light inextensible string and frictionless pulley.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both bodies accelerate with common magnitude \(a\). For the hanging block, downward is positive. For the trolley, motion to the right along the table is positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Normal force on trolley: \(N = M g = 20 \times 10 = 200\text{ N}\). Kinetic friction on trolley: \(f_k = \mu_k N = 0.04 \times 200 = 8\text{ N}\). Equation of motion for hanging block: \(mg - T = ma \implies 30 - T = 3a\). Equation of motion for trolley: \(T - f_k = Ma \implies T - 8 = 20a\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Add both equations of motion: \((30 - T) + (T - 8) = 3a + 20a \implies 22 = 23a \implies a = \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 0.96\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Now substitute \(a\) to find tension: \(T = 8 + 20 \left(\frac{22}{23}\right) = 8 + \frac{440}{23} = \frac{184 + 440}{23} = \frac{624}{23} \approx 27.13\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verify: \(30 - 3(0.9565) = 30 - 2.87 = 27.13\text{ N}\). Thus, \(a = \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 0.96\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(T \approx 27.1\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(a = \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 0.96\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(T \approx 27.1\text{ N}\)

answer.text: \(a = \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 0.96\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(T \approx 27.1\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q38 - Tension in connecting string between two pulled blocks

questiontext.text: Two blocks of masses \(m_A = 10\text{ kg}\) and \(m_B = 20\text{ kg}\) resting on a smooth horizontal surface are connected by a light string. A horizontal force \(F = 600\text{ N}\) is applied to block A away from B, and in a second case the same force \(F = 600\text{ N}\) is applied to block B away from A. What are the tensions in the string in the first and second cases, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Masses: \(m_A = 10\text{ kg}\), \(m_B = 20\text{ kg}\). Applied force: \(F = 600\text{ N}\). Smooth surface (frictionless). Light connecting string.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Total mass of the system: \(M_{\text{total}} = m_A + m_B = 10 + 20 = 30\text{ kg}\). The system accelerates as a whole in the direction of the applied force.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
System acceleration: \(a = \frac{F}{m_A + m_B}\). The tension in the string provides the accelerating force to the trailing block.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
System acceleration in both cases: \(a = \frac{600\text{ N}}{30\text{ kg}} = 20\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Case 1 (force applied to A): block B is the trailing block pulled solely by the tension \(T_1\). Therefore, \(T_1 = m_B a = 20\text{ kg} \times 20\text{ m s}^{-2} = 400\text{ N}\). Case 2 (force applied to B): block A is the trailing block pulled solely by tension \(T_2\). Therefore, \(T_2 = m_A a = 10\text{ kg} \times 20\text{ m s}^{-2} = 200\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The string tension depends directly on which mass is trailing behind. Thus, the tensions are \(400\text{ N}\) when applied to A, and \(200\text{ N}\) when applied to B.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(400\text{ N}\) when applied to A, and \(200\text{ N}\) when applied to B

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q39 - Acceleration and tension in standard Atwood machine configuration

questiontext.text: Two masses of \(8\text{ kg}\) and \(12\text{ kg}\) are connected to the ends of a light inextensible string that passes over a frictionless massless pulley. Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what are the magnitude of the acceleration of the masses and the tension in the string upon release?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Masses: \(m_1 = 8\text{ kg}\) and \(m_2 = 12\text{ kg}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Pulley is frictionless and massless; string is light and inextensible.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because \(m_2 > m_1\), mass \(m_2\) accelerates downward and mass \(m_1\) accelerates upward with equal acceleration magnitude \(a\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equations of motion: for \(m_1\), \(T - m_1 g = m_1 a\); for \(m_2\), \(m_2 g - T = m_2 a\). Atwood formulas: \(a = \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) g\), and \(T = \frac{2 m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} g\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate acceleration: \(a = \left(\frac{12 - 8}{12 + 8}\right) \times 10 = \frac{4}{20} \times 10 = \frac{1}{5} \times 10 = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Calculate tension: \(T = \frac{2 \times 8 \times 12}{8 + 12} \times 10 = \frac{192}{20} \times 10 = \frac{192}{2} = 96\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verify with \(m_1\): \(T - m_1 g = 96 - 80 = 16\text{ N} = 8 \times 2\text{ N}\). Thus, \(a = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(T = 96\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(a = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(T = 96\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q40 - Weighing scale readings for person inside accelerating elevator

questiontext.text: A person of mass \(70\text{ kg}\) stands on a weighing scale inside an elevator. Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what are the readings on the scale (in newtons) when the elevator is: (i) moving upward with a uniform speed of \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\), (ii) accelerating downward at \(5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and (iii) accelerating upward at \(5\text{ m s}^{-2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of person: \(m = 70\text{ kg}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Three cases: (i) uniform upward velocity \(v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\) (acceleration \(a = 0\)), (ii) downward acceleration \(a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), (iii) upward acceleration \(a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The weighing scale records the normal contact force \(R\) exerted on the person by the platform.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Newton's second law: for upward acceleration, \(R - mg = ma \implies R = m(g + a)\); for downward acceleration, \(mg - R = ma \implies R = m(g - a)\); for zero acceleration, \(R = mg\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Case (i): \(a = 0\), so \(R_1 = 70\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 700\text{ N}\). Case (ii): downward acceleration \(a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), so \(R_2 = 70 \times (10 - 5) = 70 \times 5 = 350\text{ N}\). Case (iii): upward acceleration \(a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), so \(R_3 = 70 \times (10 + 5) = 70 \times 15 = 1050\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The scale reading equals true weight for uniform motion, decreases during downward acceleration, and increases during upward acceleration. Thus, the readings are (i) \(700\text{ N}\), (ii) \(350\text{ N}\), and (iii) \(1050\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: (i) \(700\text{ N}\), (ii) \(350\text{ N}\), (iii) \(1050\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q41 - Apparent weight of passenger in falling elevator

questiontext.text: A person of mass \(m = 70\text{ kg}\) stands on a spring balance in an elevator. If the suspension cables snap and the elevator hurtles freely downward under gravity with acceleration \(g\), what is the reading shown by the balance, and what physical state does the person experience?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of person: \(m = 70\text{ kg}\). Acceleration of the elevator: \(a = g\) directed vertically downwards.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coordinate axis: vertically downwards is taken as positive. The scale reading equals the upward normal force \(R\) exerted by the scale on the person.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Applying Newton's second law to the person in the inertial ground frame: \(mg - R = ma\). Rearranging gives: \(R = m(g - a)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
During free fall, the acceleration of the elevator is \(a = g\). Substituting this into the normal reaction formula: \(R = m(g - g) = m(0) = 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the normal contact force between the person's feet and the scale platform drops to zero, the scale reading is zero. This condition of zero apparent weight is defined as weightlessness. Thus, the reading is zero, corresponding to a state of weightlessness.

Final Conceptual Answer: Zero reading; state of weightlessness because the normal reaction between the person and the balance becomes zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q42 - Position of body subjected to constant opposing force

questiontext.text: A body of mass \(0.40\text{ kg}\) moving initially at \(t = 0\) with a speed of \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\) along the \(+x\) direction (north) is subjected to a constant retarding force of \(8.0\text{ N}\) in the \(-x\) direction (south) for a duration of \(30\text{ s}\). Taking \(x(0) = 0\), what is the position \(x\) of the body at \(t = 25\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of body: \(m = 0.40\text{ kg}\). Initial velocity: \(u = +10\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Constant force: \(F = -8.0\text{ N}\) acting from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 30\text{ s}\). Initial position: \(x(0) = 0\). Time of evaluation: \(t = 25\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
One-dimensional motion along the \(x\)-axis. North is \(+x\) and south is \(-x\). Since \(t = 25\text{ s} < 30\text{ s}\), the force acts continuously throughout the motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Newton's second law: \(a = \frac{F}{m}\). Kinematic position equation: \(x(t) = ut + \frac{1}{2} a t^2\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate acceleration: \(a = \frac{-8.0\text{ N}}{0.40\text{ kg}} = -20\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Calculate position at \(t = 25\text{ s}\): \(x(25) = (10 \times 25) + \frac{1}{2} (-20) (25)^2 = 250 - 10 \times 625 = 250 - 6250 = -6000\text{ m}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The position is \(-6000\text{ m}\), indicating the body has reversed its direction of motion and traveled \(6000\text{ m}\) south of the origin. Thus, the position is \(-6000\text{ m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-6000\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q43 - Velocity of stone dropped from uniformly accelerating truck

questiontext.text: A truck starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). At \(t = 10\text{ s}\), a stone is dropped by a person standing on the top of the truck from a height of \(6\text{ m}\) above the ground. Neglecting air resistance and taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the magnitude of the velocity of the stone at \(t = 11\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Truck acceleration: \(a_{\text{truck}} = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Time of release: \(t_0 = 10\text{ s}\). Release height: \(h = 6\text{ m}\). Target instant: \(t = 11\text{ s}\) (elapsed time of free fall: \(\Delta t = 1\text{ s}\)). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coordinate system: horizontal \(x\)-axis along the direction of the truck's motion; vertical \(y\)-axis directed downwards.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
At \(t = 10\text{ s}\), the horizontal velocity of the truck is \(u_x = a_{\text{truck}} t_0\). By Newton's first law, the stone retains this horizontal velocity \(v_x = u_x\) because \(F_x = 0\) in the air. In the vertical direction, the initial vertical velocity is \(u_y = 0\), and vertical acceleration is \(a_y = g\), giving \(v_y = g \Delta t\). Total speed: \(v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Horizontal velocity: \(v_x = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 10\text{ s} = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Vertical velocity at \(\Delta t = 1\text{ s}\): \(v_y = 0 + 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 1\text{ s} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Resultant speed: \(v = \sqrt{20^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{400 + 100} = \sqrt{500} = 10\sqrt{5} \approx 22.36\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 22.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Also check vertical drop: \(y = \frac{1}{2} g (\Delta t)^2 = 0.5 \times 10 \times 1^2 = 5\text{ m} < 6\text{ m}\), so the stone has not yet hit the ground.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units and physical values are consistent. Thus, the magnitude of the velocity at \(t = 11\text{ s}\) is \(22.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(22.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q44 - Impulse calculation from piecewise linear position time graph

questiontext.text: A particle of mass \(4\text{ kg}\) moves along the \(x\)-axis. Its position-time graph shows that \(x = 0\) for \(t < 0\); \(x\) increases linearly from \(0\) to \(3\text{ m}\) between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\text{ s}\); and \(x = 3\text{ m}\) remains constant for \(t > 4\text{ s}\). What is the impulse imparted to the particle at \(t = 4\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of particle: \(m = 4\text{ kg}\). Position-time characteristics: for \(0 < t < 4\text{ s}\), the graph is a straight line from \((0, 0)\) to \((4, 3)\); for \(t > 4\text{ s}\), the graph is horizontal at \(x = 3\text{ m}\). Target instant: \(t = 4\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is strictly one-dimensional along the \(x\)-axis. Velocity is the slope of the position-time graph: \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Impulse is equal to the change in linear momentum: \(I = \Delta p = m(v_{\text{after}} - v_{\text{before}})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Velocity just before \(t = 4\text{ s}\) (slope of the line segment from \(t = 0\) to \(4\text{ s}\)): \(v_1 = \frac{3 - 0}{4 - 0} = \frac{3}{4}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Velocity just after \(t = 4\text{ s}\) (slope of horizontal line): \(v_2 = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Change in momentum at \(t = 4\text{ s}\): \(\Delta p = m(v_2 - v_1) = 4\text{ kg} \times (0 - 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}) = -3.0\text{ N s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The particle decelerates instantaneously to rest, requiring a negative impulse. Thus, the impulse imparted to the particle at \(t = 4\text{ s}\) is \(-3.0\text{ N s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-3.0\text{ N s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q45 - Impulse on ball deflected by forty five degrees

questiontext.text: A cricket ball of mass \(0.15\text{ kg}\) moving horizontally with an initial speed of \(54\text{ km h}^{-1}\) is deflected by a bat through an angle of \(45^\circ\) without changing its speed. What is the magnitude of the impulse imparted to the ball? (Given \(\sin 22.5^\circ \approx 0.3826\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of ball: \(m = 0.15\text{ kg}\). Initial and final speed: \(u = v = 54\text{ km h}^{-1} = 54 \times \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Total deflection angle between initial and final velocity vectors: \(\theta = 45^\circ\). Value given: \(\sin 22.5^\circ \approx 0.3826\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Treat the collision as planar. Impulse vector: \( \mathbf{I} = \Delta \mathbf{p} = m(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}) \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Magnitude of vector difference for two vectors of equal magnitude \(p = mu\) separated by angle \(\theta\): \(|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{p^2 + p^2 - 2p^2 \cos\theta} = 2p \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = 2 m u \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the momentum magnitude: \(p = mu = 0.15\text{ kg} \times 15\text{ m s}^{-1} = 2.25\text{ N s}\). Half angle: \(\frac{\theta}{2} = 22.5^\circ\). Calculate the magnitude of impulse: \(I = 2 \times 2.25 \times \sin(22.5^\circ) = 4.50 \times 0.3826 \approx 1.7217\text{ N s} \approx 1.72\text{ N s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check limiting values: if deflected by \(180^\circ\), \(I = 2p = 4.50\text{ N s}\). For \(45^\circ\), \(I = 1.72\text{ N s}\). Thus, the magnitude of the impulse is \(1.72\text{ N s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(1.72\text{ N s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q46 - Maximum whirling speed under string breaking tension

questiontext.text: A stone of mass \(0.25\text{ kg}\) tied to the end of a string is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius \(1.5\text{ m}\) on a frictionless horizontal plane. If the string can withstand a maximum tension of \(200\text{ N}\), what is the maximum linear speed with which the stone can be whirled without breaking the string?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of stone: \(m = 0.25\text{ kg}\). Radius of circular path: \(R = 1.5\text{ m}\). Maximum allowable tension: \(T_{\max} = 200\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is in a horizontal plane where the string tension provides the necessary centripetal force directed towards the center.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Centripetal force formula: \(T = \frac{m v^2}{R}\). At maximum tension: \(T_{\max} = \frac{m v_{\max}^2}{R} \implies v_{\max} = \sqrt{\frac{T_{\max} R}{m}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values: \(v_{\max}^2 = \frac{200\text{ N} \times 1.5\text{ m}}{0.25\text{ kg}} = \frac{300}{0.25} = 1200\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\). Compute the square root: \(v_{\max} = \sqrt{1200} = \sqrt{400 \times 3} = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 20 \times 1.732 = 34.64\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 34.6\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check units: \(\sqrt{\frac{\text{N} \cdot \text{m}}{\text{kg}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s}^{-2}}{\text{kg}}} = \text{m s}^{-1}\). Thus, the maximum linear speed is \(34.6\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(34.6\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q47 - Action force on yielding floor by accelerating system

questiontext.text: A wooden block of mass \(2\text{ kg}\) rests on a soft horizontal floor. An iron cylinder of mass \(25\text{ kg}\) is placed on top of the block, causing the floor to yield steadily such that the block and cylinder accelerate downwards together at \(0.1\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the magnitude of the force exerted by the block on the floor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of block: \(m_1 = 2\text{ kg}\). Mass of cylinder: \(m_2 = 25\text{ kg}\). Total mass of system: \(M = m_1 + m_2 = 2 + 25 = 27\text{ kg}\). Downward acceleration: \(a = 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2}\). \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Vertical direction: downwards is chosen as the positive direction of acceleration.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Consider the composite system (block + cylinder). The external forces acting on this system are: total gravitational force \(M g\) vertically downwards, and upward normal reaction \(R'\) exerted by the floor on the block. By Newton's second law: \(M g - R' = M a \implies R' = M(g - a)\). By Newton's third law, the action force exerted by the block on the floor is equal in magnitude to \(R'\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate total weight: \(M g = 27\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 270\text{ N}\). Calculate net accelerating force: \(M a = 27\text{ kg} \times 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2} = 2.7\text{ N}\). Calculate normal reaction: \(R' = 270\text{ N} - 2.7\text{ N} = 267.3\text{ N}\). By Newton's third law, the action on the floor is directed downwards with magnitude \(267.3\text{ N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the floor yields downward, the reaction is slightly less than the static weight of \(270\text{ N}\). Thus, the force exerted by the block on the floor is \(267.3\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(267.3\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWSOFMOTION_MCQ_Q48 - Net force on particle in circular motion

questiontext.text: One end of a light string of length \(l\) is connected to a particle of mass \(m\), and the other end is tied to a small fixed peg on a smooth horizontal table. If the particle moves in a circle with constant speed \(v\), what is the net external force acting on the particle directed towards the center? (Let \(T\) be the tension in the string)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's second law of motion, \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\mathbf{a} \). In uniform circular motion of speed \(v\) and radius \(l\), the acceleration of the particle is the centripetal acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{l}\) directed towards the center.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The term \(\frac{m v^2}{l}\) represents the mass times acceleration product (\(m a_c\)), which is the kinematical effect of the net force, not a physical force itself. One should never introduce \(\frac{m v^2}{l}\) as an additional material force in an inertial frame.
